newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin conspicuous by absence from NATO summit.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin conspicuous by absence from NATO summit.

text.p: One man will be conspicuous by his absence from a NATO summit next week which will formally offer membership to several countries from eastern Europe.

Russian President Boris Yeltsin has opted not to attend the meeting in Madrid on July 8-9 despite signing a new partnership deal with NATO on May 27 which gives Moscow a say in some alliance security matters.
Yeltsin's snub signals to NATO that Russia still opposes its former Cold War foe's expansion into former communist eastern Europe and reserves the right to resist any future waves of enlargement.

"The Kremlin is sending an absolutely clear signal. Moscow is prepared to cooperate with NATO, but it has no intention of giving up its firm opposition to alliance enlargement," said Alexei Pushkov, a member of Russia's advisory Council on Foreign and Defence Policy.

The Founding Act between Russia and NATO on May 27 created a joint council for consultation on European security and enshrined close military and political cooperation, giving Russia a voice, but not a veto, in alliance decisions.

The agreement also cleared the way for NATO to invite new members to join the alliance at its summit in Madrid. Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic will duly be offered memberhsip, and other applicants will be offered at least close ties.
But Yeltsin, 66, says the new partnership does not mean Russia accepts NATO expansion. He still regards enlargement as a security threat which will open new divisions in Europe.
"We have decided that we need a little pause after the signing of the Founding Act," Yeltsin told reporters on June 19 when he announced his decision not to attend.
"The Russians would not feel comfortable," Yeltsin said, referring to domestic opposition to NATO expansion.
Yeltsin is under pressure from communist and nationalist foes who say the deal with NATO amounts to capitulation.

"After all these years of opposing NATO expansion, Yeltsin can't just go ahead and say he subscribes to it. He wants to reserve the right to criticise it," said Andrei Kortunov, a political analyst who heads the Russian Science Foundation.

"He would have been in a weak position if he had gone to Madrid. If he had expressed his opposition to expansion there, and then it went ahead, it would have looked like he was being overruled. It would have looked very bad back home."
Yeltsin is sending deputy prime minister Valery Serov and deputy foreign minister Nikolai Afanasevsky to represent Russia in Madrid -- a relatively low-level delegation.
Afanasevsky was involved in the negotiations on the NATO-Russia partnership deal and is qualified to take part in any discussion in Madrid of how the partnership is working out.

Serov is chairman of a Russian-Spanish commission on economic cooperation, but is better known as one of the architects of a recent union pact deepening integration between Russia and the former Soviet republic of Belarus.
Some political analysts regard Russia's increasing ties with Belarus as a response to NATO expansion and suggest the choice of Serov is also a signal to the West to tread cautiously.
"I think the choice of Serov is deliberate. He is a seen as a relative hardliner who wants to promote integration with other post-Soviet countries," Kortunov said.

Russia has opted for cooperation with NATO, but has made clear it will resist any attempts by the alliance to include former Soviet republics in future waves of expansion. This risks turning into the next major dispute between Russia and NATO.

Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov has said Russia will review its relations with NATO if the alliance tries to lure in ex-Soviet republics, and is particularly sensitive over Ukraine and the Baltic states of Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia.
